tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

## Blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

4	
5	This part tests the home blood-pressure step loop as a strategy partner and an early-stage deep-tech investor would: one governing question, the choices, money, forces, risks and the next 90 days. Claims-check corrections (D3-01 to D3-03) are applied; judgements carry OUR VIEW.

7	### G2. The question tree
8	
9	The governing question: "Can a medicine-adjusting loop that starts with blood pressure become a business that improves outcomes for people far from a specialist?" Six sub-questions follow, each graded strong, partial or missing.
10	
11	| Sub-question | What the research supports | Evidence |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| 1. Does the loop work? | Abroad, yes, in randomised trials. US, HyperLink: 450 adults, pharmacists adjusting doses from home readings against usual care, 57.2% against 30.0% controlled at 6 and 12 months [D1-01-F04]. Lesotho: 547 adults, lay workers adjusting one pill with an app against referral to a clinic, 58% against 48% controlled at 12 months [D3-05-F24]. India's nearest trial was null: mWellcare, 3,698 people at 40 health centres, 12 months, a decision-support app at the visit against enhanced usual care, systolic (the upper number) 0.98 mmHg apart, not significant [D1-01-F46]. No Indian randomised trial of the home loop was found (D1-01). | Strong abroad; missing in India |
14	| 2. Is the gap real in India? | Yes. At 24 government-programme clinics 51% of 21,895 registered patients returned; among them control rose from 26.3% to 59.8% (no comparison group) [D1-03-F10]. The cause is less clear: of 157 lapsed patients phoned in Bathinda (not a random sample), 24.8% felt no illness and 22.2% named distance [D3-05-F07]. | Strong on size; partial on cause |
15	| 3. Can it be delivered safely and legally? | Safety: in rural China (33,995 people, 4 years) dose-stepping by village doctors under physician supervision brought no more falls, low pressure or kidney harm than in comparison villages [D1-01-F38]. Law: CDSCO (India's device regulator) lists hypertension platforms as medical device software (July 2026 guidance) [D2-04-F07]; the risk class and the pilot permit are questions for counsel and CDSCO [D2-04-F06, D2-04-F14]. The 2020 telemedicine guidelines say only a registered doctor may prescribe and must deliver the prescription directly [D2-04-F17]. No order letting a nurse change a dose was found [D2-04-F18]. | Partial |
16	| 4. Will anyone pay? | No Indian payer was found paying for remote monitoring or digital therapy as a line item [D2-04-F47]. Our ₹149 a month is an ASSUMPTION (DT3). | Missing |
17	| 5. Can it be defended? | Not yet. The protocol is public [D1-06-F14]. The government programme (over 2.5 million patients by April 2022) runs on the open-source Simple app, whose protocol model has no step ladder [D2-01-F12, D1-06-F40]. | Missing |
18	| 6. Can this team start it? | The prototype, yes: the protocol and open readings exist [D1-06-F14, D2-03-F61]. A pilot needs a supervising doctor, an ethics committee and prior registration (search summary only) [D2-04-F45]; the team has none yet. | Partial |
19	
20	So what for us (OUR VIEW): the medicine is settled; payment and defence are not.

49	
50	This follows the rupee along the chain and names the pool a loop could draw on.
51	
52	- **Medicines.** The largest pool: about ₹16,371 crore of blood-pressure medicines sold through chemists (Pharmarack, year to December 2025) [D2-05-F01]. One private-brand combination pill a day costs about ₹3,906 a year (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹10.7 x 365, 2019-20 prices) [D2-05-F17].
53	- **Devices.** Small and one-time: a cuff costs about ₹2,600 (2026 listings, search summary only) [D1-06-F31].
54	- **Consultations.** No checked figure in the notes.
55	- **Programmes.** Diabetes only, loss-making: Sugar.fit earned ₹66.5 crore and lost ₹42 crore in the year to March 2025 [D2-05-F19]. Blood-pressure programme revenue: no figure.
56	
57	Which pool (OUR VIEW). A loop can draw on what a clinic or hospital earns by keeping a patient, or on a medicine maker's patient-support budget (size NOT FOUND). On our model (DT3: OUR ARITHMETIC, ₹149 a month ASSUMPTION) the reachable market is ₹749 crore, under 5% of the pill pool (749 ÷ 16,371), and year-5 revenue is ₹17.9 crore. 119	Each has the honest answer and what would settle it.

7	### The option tree
8	
9	The options are grouped by what the feedback loop changes; seven were scored (A to G). The rest were weighed and left out, and each reason given is OUR VIEW.
10	
11	- **1. A drug dose or a protocol step**
12	  - **A. Blood pressure**, from a home cuff. Scored 4.35. Card 1.
13	  - **B. Insulin dose in type 2 diabetes**, from fasting sugar. Scored 3.35. Card 2.
14	  - **G. Heart-failure medicines**, from weight, pressure, pulse and lab values. Scored 3.10. Card 4.
15	  - **C. Breathing plan for asthma and COPD (long-term lung disease)**, from an inhaler sensor, peak flow (how hard a person can blow out) and air quality. Scored 3.05. Card 5.
16	  - **F. Warfarin (a blood thinner)**, from a home INR test (a blood test of clotting time). Scored 2.90. In a pooled review (28 trials, 8,950 people), the trials where patients tested at home and set their own dose showed fewer clots (risk ratio 0.47; below 1 means fewer) and fewer deaths (0.55) than usual care [D1-02-F05].
17	  - **E. Weight-loss injection dose**, from weight and side effects. Scored 2.70. No outcome evidence for digital dose support was found; an independent US review is due in 2027 [D1-01-F41].
18	  - **Gout medicine**, from blood urate. Not scored: the one trial found had nurses stepping the dose, with no device or software [D1-02-F06].
19	- **2. Food and behaviour**
20	  - **Meals guided by a glucose sensor.** Not scored: Indian programmes already sell this with a doctor and a coach [D1-04-F04, D1-04-F06, D1-04-F07].
21	  - **Lifestyle coaching app for blood pressure.** Not scored: it changes no medicine. Japan has insured one, CureApp HT, since 1 September 2022 [D1-01-F57].
22	  - **Activity nudges.** Not scored: in a 6-week trial of 44 US adults, the effect on steps faded [D1-02-F31, D2-03-F02].
23	- **3. Exercise as the dose**
24	  - **D. Rehabilitation at home**, guided by camera and pulse sensor. Scored 3.35. Card 3.
25	- **4. Therapy delivered by the device itself**
26	  - **Closed-loop insulin pumps.** Not scored: costly hardware. One maker, Insulet, reported US$842.0 million of revenue in the third quarter of 2026 [D1-05-F41].
27	  - **Wearable nerve stimulation for migraine.** Not scored: the patient triggers it and no sensor closes the loop [D1-02-F12].
28	  - **Auto-adjusting breathing machines.** NOT RESEARCHED.
29	- **5. Biofeedback**
30	  - **Device-guided slow breathing for blood pressure.** Not scored: across 8 trials (494 people, up to 9 weeks) the effect vanished once the 5 trials tied to the maker were left out [D1-02-F11].

187	#### S.M.A.R.T problem statement
188	
189	To stop blood pressure staying high because the dose change waits for a visit that half the patients never make [R], doctors in private clinics and their patients on blood-pressure medicine [S] need the 30-day review done from home, as a doctor-approved next step of the published protocol [A], shown in one clinic over a 90-day pilot [T], measured by the share of patients under 140/90 and bought at ₹149 a patient a month (ASSUMPTION) [M].
190	
191	- **S · Specific:** one buyer (a hypothesis) and one gap: the dose step between visits.
192	- **M · Measurable:** the share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned. The price is an ASSUMPTION.
193	- **A · Action-oriented:** each cycle ends in one action: step up, support, order tests, refer or hold.
194	- **R · Relevant:** 51% returned; control among them rose from 26.3% to 59.8%, with no comparison group [D1-03-F10].
195	- **T · Time-bound:** a prototype by noon on 14 November 2026; a pilot endpoint at 90 days.
196	
197	#### The belief we turn upside down
198	
199	- **Belief we turn over:** a medicine dose can change only when the patient is in front of the doctor.
200	- **Instead:** the reading travels to the doctor and the decision travels home. The 30-day review happens whether or not the patient returns.
201	
202	Why we think this solves the problem (OUR VIEW):
203	
204	- The step that fails in India is the return visit, not the protocol [D1-03-F10].
205	- Where the dose changed without a clinic visit, pressure fell [D1-01-F02, D1-01-F04].
206	- Readings alone do not do it: pooled across 15 trials (7,138 people, 12 months), self-monitoring alone gave 1.0 mmHg against usual care, no effect [D1-01-F05].
207	- The limit: prompting a clinician during a visit added nothing in mWellcare [D1-01-F46], so the value must come between visits.

16	   - Self-monitoring alone, pooled across trials: 1.0 mmHg, no effect. With intensive support (dose changes by doctors, pharmacists or patients, plus education or counselling): 6.1 mmHg (D1-01-F05).
17	   - A reminder app (MedISAFE-BP, 411 patients): 0.5 mmHg, not significant (D1-01-F06).

23	   - Heart failure: stepping drugs up fast after discharge, with four clinic visits in two months, cut death or readmission at 180 days to an adjusted 15.2% against 23.3%, with more side effects reported (41% against 29%) (D1-01-F27). 56	
57	**1. Home blood-pressure step loop (recommended).**
58	- *What it is.* A home cuff reading goes into an engine that runs India's own published step protocol: amlodipine 5 mg, then 10 mg, then add telmisartan 40 mg, then 80 mg, then add chlorthalidone 12.5 mg, with a re-check every 30 days, lab values checked before telmisartan is raised, and referral rules for very high readings, abnormal lab values and pregnancy, including women of childbearing age not on effective contraception; the sheet covers adults over 30 (Gujarat protocol, D1-06-F14). The engine proposes the next step. A doctor approves in one tap. The patient gets the change in their own language.
59	- *Why.* The strongest proof of any option, including deaths and strokes avoided at scale by non-physicians. The largest patient pool: 35.5% of Indian adults aged 20 and over have high blood pressure (D1-03-F01). The exact Indian protocol text is public. No Indian service was found.

71	
72	Build option 1. Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion.

74	- **Software:** the protocol engine, the patient chat, the doctor's approval screen, the test harness.
75	- **Hardware:** read the cuff (a phone photo of any cuff's screen, with the person confirming the digits; typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand), and build a small clip with a motion sensor that checks arm position and stillness, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change.
76	- **Biology:** encode the protocol and its safety branches, write the test cases, own the clinical story.

In its first nine districts 21.2% of people with high blood pressure are controlled [D1-01-F11]. No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the protocol model of the government's open-source app [D1-06-F40].

13	OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."

17	- **No benefit to patients has been shown.** Tonight's results are code tests, a simulation of our own, and readings from teammates.

19	- **The scores, the market model and the price are ours.** No customer has been interviewed.

But no open type 2 simulator exists (D1-06-F30), so tonight's test would be thin, and low blood sugar is a real hazard. Sanofi already has a dosing app (D1-04-F09). Best shown as the second protocol on the same engine, tested on paper.
65	
66	**3. Adaptive home rehabilitation.** The easiest demo. But software rehabilitation only matches in-person care and does not beat usual care (D1-02-F07, D1-02-F54), and Lupin says it already holds an Indian Class C device licence for cardiac rehabilitation (D1-04-F15).
67	
68	*Also weighed.* Heart failure has strong outcome proof and fits "far from a specialist" best, but it needs lab values, so it cannot be tested honestly tonight; it is the later protocol for the same engine. The breathing plan has the most hardware and the best open data, but the dose change that works in asthma needs no sensor and sensor inhalers failed commercially. Warfarin has the best proof and a small market. Weight-loss injection support is a hot market with no outcome evidence yet and three Indian players already in.
69	
70	### Recommendation
71	
72	Build option 1. Make the engine load any protocol as data, so insulin becomes "same loop, new protocol" and heart failure is the expansion.
73	
74	- **Software:** the protocol engine, the patient chat, the doctor's approval screen, the test harness.
75	- **Hardware:** read the cuff (a phone photo of any cuff's screen, with the person confirming the digits; typed entry as fallback; Bluetooth only if a suitable cuff is in hand), and build a small clip with a motion sensor that checks arm position and stillness, so a bad reading never triggers a dose change.
76	- **Biology:** encode the protocol and its safety branches, write the test cases, own the clinical story.

1	## L. Recommendation, risks and open questions
2	
3	### The recommendation
4	
5	Build the home blood-pressure step loop tonight, and present it as the first protocol on a loop that can carry others. OUR VIEW, for three reasons.
6	
7	1. **It is where the proof is strongest.** When a home reading leads to a medicine change, pressure falls by 5 to 10 mmHg more than usual care in the UK and US trials [D1-01-F01, D1-01-F02, D1-01-F04]. When health workers were allowed to step doses by protocol in rural China, heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths fell over 4 years with no rise in falls or kidney harm, though that programme also gave free or cheaper medicines and paid for results [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38]. An independent US review backed only the programmes that adjust medication [D1-01-F39].
8	2. **It is where India's gap is.** The government programme gets good control among patients who return, and about half do not return [D1-03-F10]. In its first nine districts 21.2% of people with high blood pressure are controlled [D1-01-F11]. No Indian service was found that changes a dose from home readings, and no step logic was found in the protocol model of the government's open-source app [D1-06-F40].
9	3. **It can be built and tested honestly by noon.** The state protocol is public, down to the doses and the 30-day interval [D1-06-F14]. The programme's own control-by-step figures give a base for a simulated cohort [D1-06-F04]. The build plans are in part J.
10	
11	### The pitch in one breath
12	
13	OUR VIEW. "India's own blood-pressure protocol works when patients come back, and half do not. We bring the 30-day step home: a home reading that has been checked, the state's protocol run from a data file, a doctor's one-tap approval, and the change sent in the patient's language. Before any step-up we ask whether the medicine was taken. Every branch is tested, and the same loop is ready for the next protocol."
14	
15	### What we are not claiming
16	
17	- **No benefit to patients has been shown.** Tonight's results are code tests, a simulation of our own, and readings from teammates.
18	- **It is not a medical device and not cleared by anyone.** India's July 2026 guidance treats software of this kind as a regulated device, with the class depending on how the condition is graded, and gives no exemption for tools that only a clinician sees [D2-04-F01, D2-04-F03, D2-04-F04, D2-04-F07]. A study on patients before a licence needs permission and ethics approval [D2-04-F13, D2-04-F14].
19	- **The scores, the market model and the price are ours.** No customer has been interviewed.
20	
21	### The three weak spots, said plainly
22	
23	1. **Who pays.** Public-sector medicines for blood pressure cost about ₹200 a patient a year [D2-01-F12], so a state will not pay app-scale prices. Outpatient insurance cover is tiny (search summary only) [D2-05-F10]. Our price of ₹149 a patient a month is an ASSUMPTION, and at that price the US$100 million-a-year test fails in India alone: it needs 52.7 lakh paying patients against 41.9 lakh in the serviceable market (OUR ARITHMETIC, part F2). The companies that died abroad sold software without a payer [D1-02-F42, D1-02-F44].
24	2. **It will be regulated.** See above. The honest path is clinician-approved proposals at one partner clinic under ethics approval, then a licence.
25	3. **An Indian trial of clinic decision support found nothing.** In mWellcare, prompting nurses and doctors during visits added 0.98 mmHg, not significant, over well-run usual care [D1-01-F46]. Our loop has to earn its value between visits and among the patients who do not return. If a pilot shows no gain in return rate or control, that is the result that stops the project.
26

19	#### (a) What gets built
20	
21	OUR DESIGN, from the two build notes:
22	
23	- **The engine.** One pure Python function, `decide()`, reads a protocol file (YAML, a plain-text data format), the patient's state and the week's readings, and returns a proposal with reasons. No input or output, no clock, no randomness. It never computes a dose; it can only pick a regimen written in the file. No language model in the dose path. Stack: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite, pydantic, pytest.
24	- **Three screens.** (1) Patient: Telegram chat, same flow on a web form as fallback: measure prompt, photo or typed entry, adherence buttons, change message. (2) Clinician queue: cards sorted urgent first, with step, 7-day sparkline, mean, adherence answer, quoted protocol line, guards ticked, proposed regimen, and Approve, Edit, Reject; a timer is logged. (3) Results: tests, coverage, simulation chart, live-run counts, approve times, protocol dropdown.
25	- **The reading route.** Every route writes {sys, dia, pulse, time, source, quality_flag}. D2-02's order for tonight: a phone photo of any cuff's screen, read by a vision model and confirmed by the patient; an Omron HEM-7156T over Bluetooth with omblepy, only if one is in hand by about 02:00 [D2-02-F1]; typed entry, always built. Photos are read twice, checked for plausible ranges, and shown back for confirmation. Purpose-trained readers reached 0.9-1.2 mmHg mean systolic error on held-out sets, but about 82% of one Guatemalan field set were poor-quality images and errors clustered in the last digit [D2-02-F4]; general vision models are untested on cuff screens [D2-02-F8].
26	- **The quality clip.** An ESP32 with two MPU6050 motion sensors, on the cuff (0x68) and a wrist strap (0x69), on GPIO21 and GPIO22. It enforces 300 seconds of still rest, checks the forearm is near horizontal (within 20 degrees) and the upper arm within 15 degrees of a calibrated posture, holds stillness through each 60-second reading, and posts a valid flag with reasons. It does not measure blood pressure. It targets arm hanging at the side (+6.5/+4.4 mmHg) and arm on the lap (+3.9/+4.0) against arm on a desk, from a crossover randomised trial of 133 adults in Baltimore [D2-02-F16]. Unsensed errors (legs crossed, clothing, cuff size, talking) go into a phone checklist.

84	#### (c) The decision in plain steps
85	
86	1. If the patient is referred or waiting for lab results, do nothing. If the patient is outside the sheet's population (30 or under on the Gujarat file), or has diabetes, a past heart attack or stroke, or kidney disease, flag "outside the demo, send to the doctor": the sheet has branches for these that tonight's engine does not handle [D1-06-F14].
87	2. Keep only readings that passed the quality gate.
88	3. Safety first. Newest session at or above 180 systolic or 110 diastolic: ask for a repeat after rest; if confirmed, raise an urgent card and tell the patient to contact the clinic today. This beats the 30-day wait. The low-pressure branch fires only once a clinician sets its threshold.
89	4. Fewer than 3 valid days: ask for more readings.
90	5. Fewer than 30 days on the step: "keep going".
91	6. Home mean below 135/85: "same medicine", no doctor needed.
92	7. At or above the line: ask the adherence question. Any missed day, or no tablets left: send support, no step-up, card to the clinician for information.
93	8. On the last step: propose referral.
94	9. Pregnant, or a woman of childbearing age not on effective contraception, and the next step has a barred drug (telmisartan, chlorthalidone, or any ACE inhibitor, ARB, thiazide-type diuretic or statin): propose referral. Amlodipine steps may go ahead; uncontrolled on the intensified amlodipine dose: propose referral [D1-06-F14]. Labs missing before telmisartan 80: propose a lab order. Any lab value abnormal: propose referral, or, if no specialist can be reached, propose withdrawing telmisartan and adding chlorthalidone [D1-06-F14].
95	10. Otherwise propose the next step, quoting the sheet line. Nothing that changes treatment reaches the patient before a clinician approves.

97	The adherence question is two chat buttons: "In the last 7 days, how many days did you miss your BP tablet? 0 / 1-2 / 3 or more" and "Do you have tablets left for the next 7 days? yes / no". 99	#### (d) The home-reading rule
100	
101	- **Block:** on days 24 to 30 of each 30-day cycle, two readings 1 minute apart after 5 minutes seated rest, morning before tablets and evening [D2-01-F1, D2-02-F10].
102	- **Valid session:** both readings pass the quality flags; its value is their mean.
103	- **Enough:** at least 3 distinct valid days, aiming for 7. ESH (the European Society of Hypertension) says "Seven-day monitoring (not fewer than 3 days)" [D2-01-F1].
104	- **Day 1:** dropped only if 4 or more valid days remain. ESH calls dropping it a "matter of debate" [D2-02-F12]; the AHA notes some guidelines drop it [D2-02-F10].
105	- **Still high (the home threshold):** mean systolic at or above 135 OR mean diastolic at or above 85. ESH says home 135/85 corresponds to office 140/90 [D2-01-F1]; ISH says home hypertension is readings "consistently 135/85 mm Hg or greater" [D2-01-F3]; the Indian Guidelines IV give above 135/85 (search summary only) [D2-01-F4, D2-02-F15].
106	- **Very high:** any single session at or above 180 or 110.
107	- **Clinic reading in the cycle:** the card shows both; the clinician decides.
108	
109	The Gujarat sheet is written for clinic readings ("SBP 140 or DBP 90") [D1-06-F14]. **Mapping a clinic protocol to home readings at 135/85 is OUR DESIGN.** Say so aloud on the slide, and keep the threshold a protocol value the clinician signs. No Indian home-against-clinic offset was searched.

289	### 7. The hardest questions
290	
291	Six questions the notes expect from a deep-tech fund, with short answers.
292	
293	**Software (D2-01)**
294	
295	1. *"This is a rules engine. Where is the deep tech, and what stops Simple copying it?"* The dose logic should be rules, because the evidence comes from protocol titration [D1-01-F09, D1-01-F38]. The hard parts are trusting a home reading from any cuff, choosing between stepping up and fixing intake, and a dataset of approved steps with their 30-day response that nobody in India holds [D1-06-F42]. Simple's protocol model stores a drug list and follow-up days, and no step logic was found in it [D1-06-F40]; we aim to plug into it.
296	2. *"What measurable impact, and how soon?"* Tonight: code correctness and a simulation only. The endpoint is the share of enrolled patients controlled plus the return rate, against IHCI's 51% return and 21.2% district control [D1-03-F10, D1-01-F11]. A US programme reported -8.7 mmHg at 6 months against education alone, non-randomised, with about 45% dropped out or unreachable [D2-01-F5], so engagement is the number to watch.
297	3. *"Who pays, and is this a medical device?"* Probably a device. CDSCO's software guidance was issued 21 Jul 2026 [D2-04-F01] (D2-01 still had the 21 Oct 2025 draft [D2-01-F11]) and names a hypertension digital therapeutic as device software [D2-04-F07]; the D2-04 note reads a doctor-approved step proposal as Class B, or A, with CDSCO confirming the class [D2-04-F06]. First payer: a private clinic chain at about ₹149 per patient a month (ASSUMPTION), since public drugs cost about ₹200 per patient per year [D2-01-F12].
298	
299	**Hardware (D2-02)**
300	
301	4. *"Your clip measures angles, not heart level."* It compares each reading with a supervised reference posture and catches the two errors with published sizes [D2-02-F16]. Its tolerance is about 1 mmHg of height shift (OUR ARITHMETIC at 0.49 mmHg per cm [D2-02-F17]). Legs, clothing, cuff size and talking are checklist items. Tonight shows only whether it separates deliberately wrong posture on a few teammates.
302	5. *"Patients can photograph an old reading, and the model can misread."* Trained readers reach about 1 mmHg error on good images, but field images are often poor [D2-02-F4] and general models are untested [D2-02-F8]. So reads are shown back, two must agree, memory screens are rejected, a step needs at least 3 days, and the doctor approves. A photo cannot prove who or when; the clip time-join narrows that gap without closing it.
303	6. *"Is a ₹2,000 cuff accurate enough, in Indian arms?"* Use listed cuffs: the HEM-7120 passed ESH-IP 2010 [D2-02-F28]; a popular Indian model is listed as not validated [D2-02-F32]. Cuff size matters more: a regular cuff reads +4.8 mmHg on large arms and +19.5 on extra-large arms [D2-02-F19], so the app asks arm size and refuses out-of-range arms. Validation in Indian populations was not found.

307	OUR DESIGN, built only from what the notes support. It asks whether the loop survives normal clinic work, not whether it lowers pressure.

309	- **Setting:** one clinic; a small number of adults already on step 1 or 2; their own doctor reviews every proposal in a normal consultation; written consent naming the software, as ICMR's AI guidance expects consent and a human in control [D2-04-F35]. Under the telemedicine guidelines only a registered doctor may counsel or prescribe, and the final prescription or counselling "has to be directly delivered by the RMP" (registered medical practitioner; clause 5.4) [D2-04-F17]. OUR DESIGN, a question for a lawyer: the approval and the patient message are the doctor's own act, sent in the doctor's name.

317	
318	OUR DESIGN throughout unless cited.
319	
320	**Primary endpoint:** the share of all enrolled patients with a home mean under 135/85 at 90 days; patients who stop sending readings count as not controlled. Why: it can move within three 30-day steps; control is what India's programme already reports [D1-01-F11]; and counting silent patients tests the loop where mWellcare did not look, between visits and among the 49% who do not return [D1-01-F46, D1-03-F10].

326	| Design | Can show | Cannot show |
327	|---|---|---|
328	| Before and after | Change against the clinics' own past | Whether it would have happened anyway |

88	OUR VIEW, five points:
89	
90	1. **One outcome, measured one way.** Share under 140/90 at 90 days among patients who would not have returned (51% return today) [D1-03-F10]; a US review counted a 5 mmHg systolic fall as meaningful [D1-01-F39]. Show how each home reading is checked for posture and repeats.
91	2. **The easiest wedge.** His partner asks for the "easiest" wedge into a large market [D2-07-F14]. Blood pressure is it: 35.5% of Indian adults 20 and over [D1-03-F01], a cuff at about ₹2,600 (search summary only) [D1-06-F31], and a step protocol already in government text [D1-06-F14]. 92	3. **Prototype to product.** Tonight: every protocol branch tested, a clinician approving each change. Next: a 90-day pilot. 93	4. **A real Japan angle.** Name only Panasonic's health and wellness theme [D2-07-F9], the CII delegation and the Intralink event. Claim no Japanese partner.

1	# SPARK Night 2026: the adaptive care challenge, told as one story
2	
3	**What this is.** The working document for the Beyond Next Ventures challenge at SPARK Night (13-14 Nov 2026, Ashoka University), rewritten on 14 November so that it reads in one line from start to finish. It is the same research as the 13 November edition, in a new order. Nothing was researched again, no fact was changed and nothing was added. Repeated passages were removed, and each topic now sits in one place. Internal to the team.
4	
5	**Status.** The research was completed on 13 Nov 2026 at about 11:10 PM. Three claims checks re-opened the sources of about 183 load-bearing facts, and their corrections are applied throughout. Chapter 7 says what was not checked and what was not found.
6	
7	**The challenge, as set by the fund.**
8	
9	> We need ways to manage chronic disease burden at scale despite limited access to resources, specialists and irregular clinical follow-ups. Patients need treatment methods that responds to their specific condition, and will remain adaptive to patient needs between appointments. How can digital therapeutics use rapid feedback from medical devices or biomarkers to continuously personalise care, thereby bringing measurable improvements in health outcomes to patients who cannot access frequent specialist support? The opportunity is to extend effective treatment into everyday life, beyond monitoring and reminders.
10	
11	### How the document is laid out
12	
13	The story comes first, in the order the argument builds. The answer comes at the end of the story, not at the start. The appendix holds the full detail behind each chapter, each topic in one place.
14	
15	| Chapter | The question it answers | Full detail in |
16	|---|---|---|
17	| 1. The problem | What is the fund asking, who is it about, why does care break down between visits, and why has the market not fixed it | Appendix A |
18	| 2. What the research found | What actually improves outcomes, how care has been scaled without specialists, what the technology can do, who else is doing this, where the money is, and what the rules say | Appendices B, C, D, E |
19	| 3. Analysis: what it all means | Where to play, how to win, which of the options to build and why | Appendix F |
20	| 4. The product we can build | What the home blood-pressure step loop is and how it works for the patient and the doctor | Appendix G |
21	| 5. The MVP | What gets built tonight, what can honestly be shown at noon, and what comes after | Appendix G |
22	| 6. Recommendation, risks and open questions | What to do, how to pitch it, its weak spots, and what the team still has to decide (the old part L) | Appendix H |
23	| 7. Method and limits | How this was made and how far to trust it (the old part M) | Appendix I |
24	
25	### Which part to read
26	
27	| If you are | Read |
28	|---|---|
29	| Anyone on the team, first time | Chapters 1 to 6, in order |
30	| Building the engine and screens | Chapters 4 and 5, then Appendix G, then Appendix C |
31	| Building the hardware | Chapter 5, then Appendix G (parts and the hardware test), then Appendix C (sensing and reading quality) |
32	| The biology student | Chapters 2.1 and 2.2, then Appendix B, then Appendix G (the protocol file and the test cases) |
33	| Leading the pitch | Chapters 1 to 6, then Appendix H (the mentor) and Appendix F (strategy and options) |
34	| Writing the one-page thesis | Appendix G (the draft), chapter 1 (the argument), Appendix A (the numbers) |
35	| Asked "who else is doing this" | Chapter 2.4, then Appendix D |
36	| Asked "how big is it" or "is it legal" | Chapters 2.5 and 2.6, then Appendix E |
37	
38	### How to trust a number here
39	
40	- **Every fact carries an ID that links to its source**, for example D1-01-F02. Appendix I is the register: what each research note recorded, the link, whether the page was opened or only seen in a search summary, and the verdict of the claims check where one was run. Numbers were read at source by one research agent; the load-bearing ones were then re-checked by a second.
41	- **"Search summary only"** marks a fact seen only in a search result, not on the page itself.
42	- **Some statements are ours, and marked so:** OUR VIEW (a judgement), OUR ARITHMETIC or OUR ESTIMATE (a sum or a guess from stated inputs), ASSUMPTION (an input we chose), OUR DESIGN (a design choice of ours), THEIR CLAIM (a company about itself), EXAMPLE (mock-up data). The option scores, the market model, the simulation and the price are all ours.
43	- **Mock-up screens show example data.** Every name and reading in them is invented.
44	- **What was not done:** no customer interviews; no measured split of public and private treatment; no current specialist counts; no Indian trial of home readings driving dose steps was found. Each appendix ends with what it could not find.
45	- **It is not medical or legal advice.** The legal sections say what the texts say and list the questions for a lawyer.

47	### 4. Market size, counted two ways
48	
49	![Market size, counted two ways](adaptive-care-pictures/23-market-size.png)
50	*Chart: the levels used after counting each two ways. OUR ARITHMETIC; several inputs are assumptions.*
51	
52	All figures here are OUR ARITHMETIC from our market model (DT3), in rupees a year, at ₹149 a patient a month, ₹1,788 a year (ASSUMPTION, from the build plan). Each level is counted top-down and bottom-up, and the lower figure is used so the case does not rest on the kinder count.
53	
54	| Level | Top-down | Bottom-up | Used (the lower) |
55	|---|---|---|---|
56	| TAM: every Indian adult on blood-pressure medicines who could be served (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹7,494 crore (419.1 lakh private retail patients) | ₹9,969 crore (557.5 lakh treated adults, low case) | **₹7,494 crore** |
57	| SAM: private patients a doctor could enrol on a household smartphone (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹1,668 crore (93.3 lakh patients through 3.1 lakh doctors) | ₹749 crore (41.9 lakh patients) | **₹749 crore** |
58	| SOM year 3 (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹3.7 crore (0.5% of SAM) | ₹2.1 crore (60 clinics x 200 patients) | **₹2.1 crore** |
59	| SOM year 5 (OUR ARITHMETIC) | ₹22.5 crore (3% of SAM) | ₹17.9 crore (400 clinics x 250 patients) | **₹17.9 crore** |
60	
61	(TAM: total market; SAM: the part we could serve; SOM: the part we could win.)
62	
63	**How each figure is counted.**
64	- **TAM top-down.** Retail blood-pressure medicine sales ₹16,371 crore [D2-05-F01] divided by a private patient's yearly medicine spend ₹3,906 [D2-05-F17] = 419.1 lakh patients buying in the private market. Times ₹1,788 a year = ₹7,494 crore. The spend figure is a modelled price for one brand pill a day; across the paper's range of about ₹2,500 to ₹5,100 the count runs from 321.0 lakh to 654.8 lakh patients [D2-05-F17].
65	- **TAM bottom-up.** 315 million adults with high blood pressure (a 2021 projection by the survey's investigators, not a count) [D1-03-F02] x 17.7% on medicines (NFHS-5 2019-21, preprint) [D1-03-F07] = 557.5 lakh (the ceiling from drug sales, 30.7%, a 2018 ceiling that assumes the public sector gives 30% of treatment [D2-05-F30], would give 967.0 lakh). Times ₹1,788 = ₹9,969 crore.
66	- **SAM bottom-up.** 419.1 lakh private patients x 50% reachable on a household smartphone x 20% whose doctor could enrol them (both ASSUMPTION) = 41.9 lakh patients. Times ₹1,788 = ₹749 crore.
67	- **SAM top-down.** 13,88,185 registered doctors (reply to Parliament, December 2025) [D2-05-F38] x 80% in practice x 70% private x 40% managing blood pressure = 3.1 lakh doctors, x 30 patients each = 93.3 lakh patients. Times ₹1,788 = ₹1,668 crore. The 80% is the ministry's own availability assumption, for allopathic and AYUSH doctors together; the rest are ASSUMPTION. Beside our 70% private: the notes have 11% of registered doctors in government in 2018, and "more than 80%" private in an NSSO-based study (search summary only) [D3-07-F08]. The model has not been rerun with these.
68	- **SOM bottom-up.** Clinics live and paying patients per clinic at each year end; the first year is an unpaid pilot (all ASSUMPTION):
69	
70	| Year | Clinics | Patients per clinic | Paying patients | Revenue a year |
71	|---|---|---|---|---|
72	| 1 | 2 | 0 | 0 | pilot, unpaid |
73	| 2 | 15 | 150 | 2,250 | ₹0.4 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
74	| 3 | 60 | 200 | 12,000 | ₹2.1 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
75	| 4 | 180 | 220 | 39,600 | ₹7.1 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
76	| 5 | 400 | 250 | 1,00,000 | ₹17.9 crore (OUR ARITHMETIC) |
77	
78	The model leaves out public-system patients (shown in section 6), diabetes and other conditions, device sales and every country outside India.
79	
80	**The weakest inputs.** The smartphone and enrolment shares (50% and 20%) are guesses, and they set the SAM used; the 50% is in line with smartphone access of 57.9% at ages 50-59 and 44.7% at 60-69 (quoted second-hand) [D3-07-F11]. The 17.7% treated share rests on a preprint: 17.7% of all adults with hypertension treated, NFHS-5, 2019-21 [D1-03-F07]. The private count comes from medicine sales because no measured hypertension split exists; the 30.7% ceiling is built on an assumed 30% public share [D2-05-F30, D3-07-F04].
81	
82	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** The used SAM of ₹749 crore is real money but small for a venture fund. The year-5 figure of ₹17.9 crore depends entirely on how fast clinics sign.
83	
84	### 5. The US$100 million-a-year test
85	
86	The test asks whether the company could reach US$100 million of revenue a year.
87	
88	- US$100 million a year = ₹942 crore at ₹94.25 to the dollar (rate on 13 Nov 2026) (OUR ARITHMETIC).
89	- At ₹1,788 a patient a year that needs 52.7 lakh paying patients (52,71,253) (OUR ARITHMETIC).
90	- The serviceable market above holds 41.9 lakh patients. **The test fails on this model in India alone**: it needs 1.3 times the SAM (OUR ARITHMETIC).
91	
92	At higher prices fewer patients are needed: 7,85,417 at ₹1,000 a month, 3,92,708 at ₹2,000, and 3,40,136 at Omada's revenue of about US$24.5 a member a month (revenue over all members, not a price) (OUR ARITHMETIC: ₹9,42,50,00,000 divided by the yearly price) [D2-05-F23].
93	
94	Where the rest would have to come from: more protocols on the same loop (diabetes, heart failure), a paid public tier, other countries that use the same family of protocols, or a higher price paid by an insurer, employer or medicine maker.
95	
96	**So what for us (OUR VIEW).** Blood pressure in India is the entry, not the whole company. The pitch must show the same engine carrying more protocols and more payers.
97

report-parts\dtx\30-doctor.md:141:- **Warfarin.** A Cochrane review of 28 trials (8,950 patients) found that patients who tested INR at home and adjusted their own dose by a schedule had fewer clots (RR 0.47) and lower death (RR 0.55). Patients who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had fewer clots (RR 0.69) but no change in death (RR 0.94). Each approach was compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other. Major bleeding did not change overall (RR 0.95) [D1-02-F05].

Story Health as virtual teams that include a prescriber [D1-05-F1]. Cadence claims a 70% relative rise in BP control and $1,302 lower yearly cost per patient, without saying who changes the medicine (THEIR CLAIM) [D1-05-F46]. Story Health's VITAL-HF randomised 178 heart-failure patients in seven US health systems against usual care; at 6 months medicine use improved with no rise in admissions; funded by Innovaccer [D1-05-F61]. In 9amHealth's study (not randomised, 95 patients, company authors), HbA1c (average sugar over three months) fell from 8.2% to 7.2% in a year [D1-05-F60]. Virta's non-randomised study (262 against 87) cut insulin from 81.9 to 15.5 units a day (company sources, search summary only) [D1-05-F59].

30-doctor.md: Another 2026 meta-analysis of 16 trials (8,618) found a gradient: pressure-guided RR 0
30-doctor.md:68 in 16 trials with 22,748 people aged 12 and over [D1-02-F37]
---

138	
139	The other conditions repeat the pattern and add two lessons: a dose loop can work with no sensor at all, and rehabilitation by software matches in-person care without beating usual care.
140	
141	- **Warfarin.** A Cochrane review of 28 trials (8,950 patients) found that patients who tested INR at home and adjusted their own dose by a schedule had fewer clots (RR 0.47) and lower death (RR 0.55). Patients who tested at home and left the dose to the clinic had fewer clots (RR 0.69) but no change in death (RR 0.94). Each approach was compared with usual care in separate sets of trials, not with each other. Major bleeding did not change overall (RR 0.95) [D1-02-F05].
142	- **Gout.** In a UK trial (517 patients, Nottingham, 2 years), nurses titrating urate-lowering drugs to a target reached it in 95% against 30% under GP care, RR 3.18, at £5,066 per quality-adjusted life year. It was not digital: it was a protocol run by nurses [D1-02-F06].
143	- **Asthma and COPD.** SMART (one inhaler for both maintenance and relief, so each reliever puff also raises the steroid dose) cut exacerbations by RR 0.68 in 16 trials with 22,748 people aged 12 and over [D1-02-F37]. No sensor was needed because the patient's own reliever use is the signal and the inhaler delivers the dose change at that moment. Sensor inhalers did less: reminders raised adherence without changing school absence [D1-02-F01]; the Digihaler system's benefit interval crossed 1 and adherence fell from 79.2% to 68.6% over 6 months [D1-02-F02]; a Propeller trial cut reliever use but not asthma control scores overall (company-affiliated authors) [D1-02-F38]. Commercially, Teva withdrew the Digihaler app and US inhalers on 1 June 2024 [D1-02-F41], and an undated ResMed page says Propeller "has ceased operations" [D1-02-F40].
144	- **Rehabilitation by software.** Stroke telerehab after discharge was no better than usual care for daily-living activities (SMD 0.00) and about equal to in-person physiotherapy [D1-02-F07]. Lung telerehab, 99% COPD, matched centre rehab on walking distance, with completion 93% against 70% [D1-02-F03]. A Sword Health trial (140 back-pain patients, company-affiliated) found no difference in disability against in-person physiotherapy but lower dropout, 15.7% against 34.3% [D1-02-F08]. PHTI (June 2024) found physiotherapist-guided virtual care comparable to in-person care with lower spending, app-only exercise "unlikely to be effective as total substitutes", and did not separate the effect of adapting exercise to measured performance [D1-02-F54].
145	- **Biofeedback and stimulation.** Device-guided breathing lowered systolic BP by 3.67 mmHg across 8 trials, but showed no effect once the 5 manufacturer-linked trials were removed [D1-02-F11]. Nerivio, a sham-controlled migraine stimulator, gave pain relief at 2 hours in 66.7% against 38.8%, but it uses no sensor loop [D1-02-F12].
146	
147	**So what for us.** OUR VIEW: a sensor earns its place only if it changes a decision that a cheaper signal cannot. Warfarin and SMART show the dose rule itself carries the benefit.
